what_it_does: One way to make LLMs faster and cheaper to run is to use smaller numbers: instead of storing each weight (a learned parameter in the model) as a 32-bit decimal, round it to a 4-bit or 8-bit integer — a process called quantization. A popular compromise keeps weights quantized but leaves the activations (the intermediate results flowing through the network as it processes a prompt) in full floating-point precision to avoid accuracy loss. However, those full-precision activations are expensive to read from memory and expensive to multiply against quantized weights. Anda proposes a new number format for activations where a small group of numbers shares a single common exponent (the 'scale' part of the number) but each member of the group gets a variable number of mantissa bits (the precise fractional part) based on how much precision that group actually needs. An automated search algorithm figures out, without retraining the model, how many bits each layer of the network should use, trading a little accuracy for a lot of compression. On the hardware side, numbers are stored in a 'bit-plane' layout (grouping all the most-significant bits together, then all the next-significant bits, etc.) so that a 'bit-serial' compute unit — one that processes one bit-plane at a time — can skip bit-planes that contribute little to the final result, saving both time and energy.
